kit_json.name: Chart Room
kit_json.subject: Data-led briefings for staff, reporters or the public: the numbers carry the story, and every chart says where its figures came from.
kit_json.signature: A short red tab over every headline, and charts on light gridlines with the one bar that matters in red.

voice.notes: Lead with the finding, then the number that proves it. Short headlines with a verb. Say what is counted, where and when. Compare with something the reader knows. Never say a number went up without saying from what.
voice.delivery: Crisp and even, like a data reporter on the radio. Give every number room, and say what it is measured against.

kit_json.method: The data desk: a tab marker, a short headline and a standfirst that says what is measured, data in two colors, the source set small.

guide.text: These sources are a season report, a council work session transcript, and a survey on Cedar Hollow's winter warming center. Cedar Hollow is a fictional city.

chips.locator: “Cedar Hollow Winter Warming Center: Season Report, 2025-26”

guide.text: The center was open 87 nights and recorded 2,914 overnight stays by 412 different guests.
The season cost $318,400, or $109 per overnight stay, and a county grant covered $80,000.
Staff recommend opening on November 15, raising the opening trigger to 35 degrees, and adding an east side site for about $142,000.
Of the guests who answered the survey, 74 percent said getting to the center was the hardest part, and 91 percent said they felt safe.

questions.text: The second site would add $142,000 to a $318,400 season, for $460,400 in total. The $80,000 county grant won't be in writing until April. Where will the money come from?
On January 21, 61 guests stayed in a hall set up for 60. If the center opens on November 15 and at 35 degrees, can one hall handle it?
74 percent of guests said the trip to the center was the hardest part. Would an east side site fix that if no money is found for its $142,000 cost?

P1.text: Prepared by the Department of Community Services for the City Council. Cedar Hollow is a fictional city; this report is sample material for trying Imprint.
P1.locator: “Cedar Hollow Winter Warming Center: Season Report, 2025-26”

P2.text:
The warming center at the Maple Street Recreation Hall opened on the night of December 1, 2025 and closed for the season on March 15, 2026. It was open 87 nights, every night the forecast low was 32 degrees or colder, and on 9 additional nights with freezing rain.
Over the season the center recorded 2,914 overnight stays by 412 different guests. The busiest night was January 21, 2026, when 61 guests stayed during a stretch of five nights below 10 degrees. On an average night, 33 guests stayed.

P3.text: Of the 412 guests, 118 were over the age of 60 and 37 were veterans. Staff connected 64 guests with permanent or transitional housing before the season ended, up from 29 the season before.

P4.text:
The season cost $318,400. The largest costs were overnight staff at $171,900, cots, bedding and laundry at $48,200, and meals at $41,700. The cost per overnight stay was $109.
The city paid $205,000 from the general fund. A county grant covered $80,000, and private donations covered the remaining $33,400.

P5.text: Volunteers gave 3,260 hours over the season, mostly in the evening meal and morning shifts. The Cedar Hollow Faith Alliance and two neighborhood associations organized most of the volunteer schedule.

P6.text: Staff recommend opening on November 15 instead of December 1, adding a second site on the east side of the city so guests do not have to cross the river at night, and setting the opening trigger at 35 degrees instead of 32. Staff estimate the second site would add $142,000 to the season's cost.

P7.text: Mayor Okafor: Next item is the warming center season report. Director Lindqvist, go ahead. Director Lindqvist: Thank you. The short version is that the center did what it was built to do. Eighty-seven nights open, and no one was turned away for lack of space. Director Lindqvist: The night that worried us most was January twenty-first. We had sixty-one guests in a hall set up for sixty. We opened the gym as overflow and it held.

P8.text: Council Member Reyes: The east side question keeps coming up. People are walking across the Fifth Street bridge at two in the morning to get there. That is the part I can't get past. Director Lindqvist: That's why we're recommending a second site. We have a church on Ridge Avenue that has offered its fellowship hall. The estimate is about a hundred and forty-two thousand dollars for a full season.

P9.text: Council Member Pham: What I want to see before budget is where the money comes from. The county grant was eighty thousand this year. Is that renewing? Director Lindqvist: The county has told us informally they expect to renew at the same level. We won't have it in writing until April.

P10.text: Mayor Okafor: Let's put the second site and the earlier opening date on the budget work session agenda for April 8. Thank you, Director.

P11.text:
Cedar Hollow Warming Center: Guest and Volunteer Survey, March 2026
(Sample material for trying Imprint. Cedar Hollow is a fictional city.)

P12.text: The Department of Community Services surveyed guests during the last two weeks of the season and volunteers by email after it closed.

P13.text:
Guests
188 guests answered the survey. 91 percent said they felt safe at the center. 74 percent said the walk or ride to the center was the hardest part of getting there. The most requested change was earlier opening hours: the doors open at 7 p.m., and guests asked for 5 p.m. on the coldest nights.

P14.text: One guest wrote: "Having a place to go when it drops below freezing is the difference between making it through the night and not."

P15.text:
Volunteers
146 volunteers answered. 88 percent said they plan to volunteer again next season. The most common request was more training before the first night, especially on what to do in a medical emergency.
